finding.claim: /checkout computes the charge total entirely from client-supplied price and qty, so a client can pay any amount, including zero or negative.

trace.note: total = sum(i.price * i.qty) over client-supplied values, no catalog lookup
charge issued for req.user.id with the client-computed total

finding.guards_checked: None on this path: no server-side price lookup, no sign or range check on price/qty, no type check, no items array/length check. Authentication of req.user is set by middleware not present in this repo, so it is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js:4-7 has no price lookup, sign/range check, type check, or items validation. The sibling /checkout-v2 at cart.js:13-14 looks up prices via req.catalog.price(i.sku) and clamps qty, which /checkout lacks. Upstream middleware that sets req.user, req.payments, or validates req.body is not in this repo and could not be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: cart.js:5 sums client-supplied i.price * i.qty with no server-side price source, cart.js:6 charges that total, and cart.js:7 echoes it. The only plausible attacker is an authenticated customer, which is the normal role for this endpoint, so they can send a total of zero or a negative amount. The sole open question is whether app-level middleware validates req.body, and that cannot be seen from this repo, so the finding stands on the code available.

finding.claim: /checkout-v2 can pass NaN or Infinity into the charge when an sku is unknown, qty is missing or non-numeric, or qty is an out-of-range number, because Math.floor/Math.max propagate NaN and Infinity and nothing checks Number.isFinite.
finding.source: req.body.items[].qty and req.body.items[].sku (attacker-controlled); catalog.price return value for unknown sku

trace.note: p = await catalog.price(i.sku); unknown sku may yield undefined
total += p * Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty)); qty undefined gives NaN, qty 1e400 parses to Infinity, p undefined gives NaN

finding.guards_checked: No isFinite/isNaN check, no check that catalog.price returned a valid price, no sku existence check. Impact depends on how the payment provider handles NaN/Infinity, which is not in this repo (unverified).

verdict.guard_found: none: cart.js:13-14 has no isFinite/isNaN check, no validation that catalog.price returned a number, and no sku check; cart.js:12 iterates client items unvalidated; the repo contains no other middleware or validation (only cart.js and .claude skill docs exist)
verdict.reason: The trace matches cart.js:12-16: Math.floor(undefined) and an undefined catalog price yield NaN, Math.floor(Infinity) yields Infinity, and cart.js:16 charges that total with no guard in the repo, so the defect is real and reachable by any caller of /checkout-v2, but the security impact is limited because the charge goes to the requester's own account and the provider's handling of NaN/Infinity is not in this repo (unverified).

finding.claim: Math.max(1, ...) silently bills zero, negative and fractional quantities as one unit, so a 0 or 0.5 quantity is charged the full unit price. This is a business-logic error that overcharges customers.
finding.sink: total accumulation at cart.js:14 and charge at cart.js:16

trace.note: qty 0 -> floor 0 -> max(1,0)=1; qty -5 -> max(1,-5)=1; qty 0.5 -> floor 0 -> 1

finding.guards_checked: Math.max floor of 1 is the only qty control; there is no rejection of invalid quantities. Mainly a customer-overcharge defect rather than attacker profit.

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js:14 is the only qty handling (Math.max(1, Math.floor(i.qty))), and nothing in the repo validates qty. Glob shows only cart.js plus security-research skill docs, so no upstream validation middleware is visible.
verdict.reason: Trace is accurate: cart.js:14 maps qty 0 and 0.5 to 1 and -5 to 1, and cart.js:16 charges that total, with no rejection anywhere, so any authenticated user can be charged full unit price for a zero or fractional quantity. This is a correctness defect, not a security vulnerability, since the only party harmed is the requester's own cart and the attacker gains nothing. The severity should be lowered accordingly. A related point: the v1 route at cart.js:5 has no clamp at all, so negative quantities produce negative totals there.

finding.claim: Async handlers have no try/catch, so a malformed body (missing items, non-iterable items, or undefined req.user/req.payments) throws inside an async function. On Express 4 that rejection is not caught by Express, and on Node 15+ it can crash the process, a denial-of-service vector.
finding.source: Request body shape (req.body.items) and any missing middleware-populated req.user/req.payments/req.catalog
finding.sink: Unhandled promise rejection in the route handler at cart.js:5 (and cart.js:12 for v2)

trace.note: req.body.items.reduce throws TypeError when items is undefined or not an array
for...of throws TypeError on non-iterable items in checkout-v2
req.user.id throws when req.user is undefined

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no body-shape validation, no error middleware in this file. Express version (no package.json present) and any process-level unhandledRejection handler are unverified, so this depends on the deployment.

verdict.guard_found: none in cart.js: no try/catch, no body-shape validation, no error middleware. The directory has no package.json, so the Express version and any process-level unhandledRejection handler cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: cart.js:5 calls req.body.items.reduce with no guard, cart.js:6 reads req.user.id, and cart.js:12 runs for...of over req.body.items. Whether a malformed body crashes the process depends on the Express version (Express 4 does not catch async rejections, Express 5 does) and on whether a process-level unhandledRejection handler exists, and neither is visible in the available files, so the DoS cannot be confirmed or refuted from this code alone.

finding.claim: /checkout-v2 has no cap on items array length and performs one sequential catalog lookup per item, so a large items array causes unbounded work per request.
finding.sink: Sequential await req.catalog.price(i.sku) loop at cart.js:12-15

trace.note: one awaited catalog call per element, no batching or limit

finding.guards_checked: No array length limit, no deduplication, no rate limiting in this file. Body-size limits, if any, are set outside this file and are unverified.

verdict.guard_found: No array-length cap, dedupe, or rate limit in cart.js. The only candidate control is request body-size limiting, which is configured outside this directory (only cart.js is present). Express's default JSON body parser limit is 100kb, which would bound the array in practice, but I can't see whether the app uses it or sets a different limit.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: the unbounded for...of over req.body.items at cart.js:12 makes one awaited req.catalog.price call per element at cart.js:13, with no cap in the file. Whether that is "unbounded" depends on the app-level body-size limit (not in the provided files), and req.user.id at cart.js:16 suggests the route requires an authenticated user, so the attacker is a low-privilege user at most.

finding.claim: Charges are not idempotent: there is no idempotency key, no server-side order record, and no duplicate-request check, so a retried or replayed request charges again.
finding.source: Repeated identical POST to /checkout or /checkout-v2 (client retry, network replay, or double-submit)

trace.note: charge issued on every request with no dedupe key

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Any idempotency handling inside req.payments.charge is not present in this repo (unverified).

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js has no idempotency key or duplicate check (cart.js:6, cart.js:16). The repo holds only cart.js and .claude skill docs, so no payments.charge implementation exists to check for dedupe.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines exist and match the claim (cart.js:6 and cart.js:16 call req.payments.charge with no dedupe), but whether a replayed request actually double-charges depends on req.payments.charge, which is not in this repo, and the only attacker-reachable path (a victim's browser replaying POST /checkout via CSRF) depends on auth and CSRF middleware that is also absent, so the finding cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Money is computed with IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic (price * qty summed as floats), so totals can be off by fractions of a cent (for example 0.1 * 3 = 0.30000000000000004), and the charge unit (cents vs dollars) is not specified.
finding.source: price and qty values, client-supplied in /checkout and catalog-supplied in /checkout-v2
finding.sink: total passed to req.payments.charge at cart.js:6 and cart.js:16

trace.note: float total used for charge, no rounding to integer minor units

finding.guards_checked: No rounding or integer minor-unit conversion. Behavior depends on what charge() expects, which is not in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. cart.js:5 and cart.js:14-16 apply no rounding, no integer minor-unit conversion, and no validation of price types before summing, and the float total goes straight to req.payments.charge at cart.js:6 and cart.js:16.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines match the claim (cart.js:5 float multiply-and-reduce, cart.js:16 float total passed to charge with no rounding), and any caller of /checkout or /checkout-v2 can supply items, so the float total is reachable with no effective guard. The actual impact (fractional-cent error, and whether the charge unit is cents or dollars) depends on req.payments.charge, which is not in this repo, so the severity is limited even though the defect itself is confirmed.
